items.title: CBE: A Complexity-adaptive Boundary-aware Ensemble Method for Imbalanced Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.39466v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In many real-world classification tasks, datasets exhibit class imbalance, which can degrade the generalization performance of conventional learning algorithms. Data complexity has recently been recognized as a more objective indicator of learning difficulty than the imbalance ratio alone, because class overlap and complex decision boundaries often impair classifiers more severely than imbalance itself. Samples near the decision boundary are inherently difficult to classify, which has motivated many researchers to focus on such instances to improve classifier performance. However, most under-sampling approaches fail to differentiate their sampling of boundary samples across datasets of varying complexity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a complexity-adaptive boundary-aware ensemble (CBE) framework that links the sampling weight distribution to data complexity and dynamically adjusts the boundary preference of under-sampling accordingly. We also introduce an overall complexity measure that combines metrics at multiple levels and use it to divide imbalanced datasets into three categories. Extensive experiments on 24 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL show that the proposed method outperforms many existing methods in terms of F-measure and G-mean on Easy and Median datasets, without degrading performance on hard cases.
items.author: Xun Wei
items.summary: CBE is an ensemble under-sampling method for class-imbalanced classification that adapts its treatment of boundary samples based on measured data complexity (class overlap and decision-boundary difficulty) rather than imbalance ratio alone. It aims to improve generalization across datasets of varying complexity.
items.reasoning: A sensible but incremental improvement in a well-trodden area (imbalanced classification via under-sampling). The complexity-adaptive angle is a reasonable refinement, but methodological novelty and likely impact are limited.

items.title: Smartphone Indoor Localization Enhanced by Hierarchical Multi-Sensor Context Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.39691v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Smartphone indoor localization requires low-cost, robust positioning across scene transitions and phone-use variations. Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) enables infrastructure-free deployment but accumulates errors from heading drift, structural transitions, and carrying-mode changes. Existing methods often treat contextual cues as a single event stream or local correction signal, limiting their ability to address distinct localization errors. This paper presents a framework enhanced by hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition. A jointly data- and model-driven recognition model predicts environment, scene, and activity probabilities, which are converted into scene-event and action-context segments. Scene-event segments guide scene-constrained PDR correction through corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking, and vertical-transition handling. Action-context segments drive action-aware RoNIN-based position compensation for carrying-mode-dependent drift. Experiments on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references show that the proposed framework outperforms PDR and representative learned inertial odometry baselines, demonstrating that hierarchical semantics provide reliable, localization-specific correction cues.
items.author: Wenhui Feng, Muhan Weng, Jianyu Liu, Xiansheng Yang, Hao Zhang, Liang Wang, Yuan Zhuang
items.summary: This paper proposes a smartphone indoor localization framework that uses hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition to predict environment, scene, and activity probabilities, converting them into segments that constrain pedestrian dead reckoning errors. The hierarchical treatment of contextual cues addresses heading drift, structural transitions, and carrying-mode changes that degrade infrastructure-free positioning.
items.reasoning: A well-motivated applied systems paper addressing practical PDR error sources with a sensible hierarchical context model. Useful for the mobile sensing community, but the contribution is domain-specific rather than advancing core ML.

items.title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
items.content: arXiv:2610.39796v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.
items.author: Volker Kempe
items.summary: A perspective piece contrasting the enormous energy demands of connectionist AI with the low power consumption of neuromorphic approaches, focusing on spiking neural networks with local learning, event-driven computation, and time-based information coding. It argues SNNs complement rather than replace mainstream AI in hybrid systems.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important sustainability topic, but as a survey/perspective without new experiments or theoretical results, its research contribution is limited; useful background reading rather than a technical advance.

items.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
items.content: arXiv:2610.37691v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.
items.author: Zzyv Zzyzek
items.summary: This combinatorics paper settles the two-pair Zig-Zag Numberlink problem on rectangles, giving a forbidden-pattern characterization (a finite catalogue including parity and border alternation conditions), a constructive polynomial-time algorithm, and a machine-checked Lean verification for grids with both sides at least 11.
items.reasoning: Technically rigorous and commendably formalized in Lean, but a niche combinatorial result peripheral to mainstream AI/ML research; the formal verification aspect is a nice touch of methodological quality.

items.title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
items.content: arXiv:2610.37927v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.
items.author: Vishal Upendran, Banafsheh Ferdousi
items.summary: A book chapter surveying machine learning for space weather, modeling the pipeline from solar processes to ground impact as coupled systems described by state vectors. It organizes how ML can be applied to individual heliospheric systems or their couplings for forecasting near-Earth conditions.
items.reasoning: Useful domain survey with a coherent coupled-systems framing, but as a review chapter it offers limited methodological novelty and its audience is specialized.

items.title: Structural Pattern Mining in Inka Khipus: A KFG Re-Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2610.38580v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper reports a methodological pivot from the Open Khipu Repository to the Khipu Field Guide (KFG) database, prompted by stalled progress on the OKR, and a full re-analysis of the resulting 650-khipu sample. Three findings recur across every analysis attempted. First, khipu size confounds nearly every derived structural count, explaining 42-70% of its variance; all subsequent models control for it. Second, the two-letter name prefix (AS, UR, HP, QU, JC, MM, KH) identifies the original cataloger, not a site or period, which turns documentation completeness into a second confound that must be modeled explicitly. Controlling for both, khipus cataloged by Hugo Pereyra's Proyecto Quipu (HP) show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than Gary Urton's (UR) khipus (p = 0.044), while the Ascher-cataloged (AS) khipus are too collinear with their own near-total lack of side/direction documentation to assess (VIF = 5.0). Third, generic structural clustering (UMAP+HDBSCAN) does not separate the pooled 650-khipu sample from two independent null models (permutation and Gaussian), corroborating an independent conclusion already reached by the KFG itself; the same test restricted to a single cataloger (UR) proved not reproducible across runtime environments and is reported here as a methodological caveat rather than evidence of structure. A targeted replication of the KFG's own S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar/astronomical khipus recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 additional ones under the same criterion.
items.author: Maria Contreras
items.summary: This interdisciplinary work re-analyzes 650 Inka khipus (knotted-cord records) using the Khipu Field Guide database, identifying and controlling for confounds such as khipu size and cataloger identity. After correction, it finds cataloger-specific differences in structural features, including significantly fewer Ascher sum-relations for khipus cataloged by a particular project, demonstrating the need for careful statistical hygiene in computational humanities.
items.reasoning: Methodologically sound and honest about confounding, which is valuable for the emerging field of ML-assisted archaeology and khipu studies. Its impact is confined to a niche application domain, though the lesson about confound control generalizes.

items.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation of feature extractors in computer vision
items.content: arXiv:2610.39551v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Feature detection and matching are fundamental components in computer vision, underpinning a broad spectrum of applications. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of traditional feature detections and descriptors, analyzing methods such as Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), Binary Robust Independent Elementary Features (BRIEF), Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB), Binary Robust Invariant Scalable Keypoints (BRISK), KAZE, Accelerated KAZE (AKAZE), Fast Retina Keypoint (FREAK), Dense and Accurate Invariant Scalable descriptor for Yale (DAISY), Features from Accelerated Segment Test (FAST), and STAR. Each feature extractor was assessed based on its architectural design and complexity, focusing on how these factors influence computational efficiency and robustness under various transformations. Utilizing the Image Matching Challenge Photo Tourism 2020 dataset, which includes over 1.5 million images, the study identifies the FAST algorithm as the most efficient detector when paired with the ORB descriptor and Brute-Force (BF) matcher, offering the fastest feature extraction and matching process. ORB is notably effective on affine transformed and brightened images, while AKAZE excels in conditions involving blurring, fisheye distortion, image rotation, and perspective distortions. Through more than 2 million comparisons, the study highlights the feature extractors that demonstrate superior resilience across various conditions, including rotation, scaling, blurring, brightening, affine transformations, perspective distortions, fisheye distortion, and salt-and-pepper noise
items.author: Murat Isik
items.summary: This paper provides a broad empirical comparison of classical feature detectors and descriptors including SIFT, SURF, ORB, BRISK, KAZE, AKAZE, FREAK, DAISY, FAST, and STAR, assessing architectural design, complexity, and matching performance. It serves as a reference benchmark for traditional computer vision feature extraction methods.
items.reasoning: A useful survey-style empirical comparison of classical methods, but the techniques predate deep learning by a decade and single-author benchmark studies of this kind offer limited novelty; value is mainly as a reference for niche classical-vision use cases.

items.title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.40253v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.
items.author: Malte Stelzer, Marvin Sach, Timo Bartels, Dinu Mihailescu-Stoica, S\"oren Kohnert, Florian Poprawa, Marc Zeller, Tim Fingscheidt
items.summary: The paper proposes a confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimator for rail-based mobile platforms that learns from ground-facing Doppler spectra via an autoencoder, with a speed regression head on the latent features and frame-level confidence estimates. It adapts reconstruction-based performance estimation ideas to Doppler RaDAR and drops the reconstruction loss during inference. This improves reliability of speed estimation under adverse conditions where classical signal processing degrades.
items.reasoning: Competent applied ML with a nice uncertainty-awareness design for an industrial sensing problem (rail systems, credible lab with Fraunhofer-affiliated authors), but niche domain and incremental methodological novelty.

Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.

items.title: Reading-Level Verification of Kanji Words in Japanese Financial Speech Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2610.39168v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with more than one reading, such as the word for "market" (shijo vs. ichiba) or "overall trend" (taisei vs. oze), are still misread. A common quality gate transcribes each synthesized sentence with automatic speech recognition (ASR), converts both the input and the transcript to kana, and regenerates on mismatch. We show that this gate is unreliable in both directions: when the audio contains a misreading, the ASR language model frequently writes the expected kanji back, hiding the error, and when the audio is correct, ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. We propose a reading-level check that scores the expected reading and its confusable alternatives with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. On 540 utterances from three voice-cloned production voices covering 30 financial terms, with misreadings injected under controlled conditions, the transcript-based gate detected 78.9% of misreadings at a 44.4% false-alarm rate, whereas the proposed check detected 91.7% at 5.0% (AUC 0.990). On natural kanji input, it caught a front-end error that the transcript-based gate missed for one voice, and reduced regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.

items.title: Vision-Based Density Estimation for Adaptive Traffic Control
items.content: arXiv:2610.38497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Traffic congestion is becoming a critical challenge in rapidly growing urban centers, particularly in developing nations where rapid urbanization and inadequate transport infrastructure place increasing strain on transport networks. In highly heterogeneous and chaotic traffic flows, camera-based traffic-state estimation is limited by severe vehicle occlusion and overlap. In this paper, we propose a framework to optimize traffic flow directly from stochastic visual observations. The architecture is structurally decoupled into three primary components: (a) vehicle density estimation, (b) predictive dynamics modeling, and (c) policy optimization. The proposed methodology introduces a convolutional neural network (CNN) that learns the mapping from camera feeds to spatial density maps, utilizing an adaptive k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) Gaussian kernel to handle varying congestion levels. This feeds into an ST3DNet predictive module for spatiotemporal forecasting, followed by a hierarchical Graph-Transformer Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm to optimize signal phases. The density estimation stage was evaluated on 40 annotated intersection images from Rambagh 4, Jaipur, India, with a reported five-fold validation mean absolute error (MAE) of $3.32 \pm 0.95$ vehicles and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 14.5%. These results pertain to the perception component; empirical training and evaluation of the forecasting and control stages remain future work.

items.title: Assessing feature scorer results on high-dimensional datasets with t-SNE
items.content: arXiv:2610.39009v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: While vast literature on high-dimensional data visualization is available, there are not many works regarding the visualization of feature scorers and their results. Feature scorers are algorithms that assign numerical importance to each feature of multi-dimensional datasets. These importance scores can be used in several applications, such as feature selection, knowledge discovery, and machine learning interpretability. There are several feature scorers to choose from, and often no single metric or ground truth is available to guarantee the quality of their results. In this scenario, visualization can become valuable to support the decision of which method to choose and how good its results are. For this goal, this work presents "weighted t-SNE." It modifies the relationship between data points in the embedded 2D space to reflect the importance of each dimension of the original datasets as assessed by a feature scorer. This research discusses how to implement weighted t-SNE, proposes the silhouette coefficient as a numerical evaluation of the results, and shows several examples of its use in practice. Synthetic and real-world tabular datasets are used in the experiments together with nine feature scorers, ranging from Mutual Information to neural networks. Each feature scorer produces unique visualizations, and weighted t-SNE can be used to compare and choose the one that better suits a given dataset and task. Weighted t-SNE can also visually show the importance of features learned by machine learning models and help us see how they are organizing the data, increasing their interpretability.

items.summary: This paper addresses the underexplored problem of visualizing and assessing the outputs of feature scorers, algorithms that assign importance values to features in high-dimensional datasets. The authors propose a weighted visualization approach built on t-SNE to help practitioners compare feature scoring methods and judge result quality when no ground truth exists. This supports downstream tasks like feature selection and model interpretability.

The work fills a genuine gap in the interpretability literature, but relies on established techniques (t-SNE) and offers limited evidence of broad impact. Novelty and expected influence are modest compared to major-lab research or new architectures.

items.title: Value Probes: Learned Value Functions for Beam-Search Red Teaming
items.content: arXiv:2610.38526v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated red-team auditing of language models is an important way to evaluate safety-relevant behaviors. These audits implicitly search a tree of possible conversation pathways: at each turn an auditor model decides which conversation to continue, and an LLM judge scores the dialogue. We emphasize that this auditing procedure is a Markov decision process, where states are the conversation history, actions are candidate responses, and rewards are judge scores for the target behavior. By adopting this perspective, we introduce two major improvements to auditing. First, we propose adopting beam search for the audit rather than relying on the auditor alone. We then interpret the problem of finding states that are likely to lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. Surprisingly, we show that this value function can be estimated by linear probing from the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards - a method we term "Value Probes." By using Value Probes as a heuristic in our beam-search audit, we are able to substantially improve auditing success. Across 18 target behaviors and 3 scales of models, our approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared to (token-matched) standard auditing approaches. Furthermore, we show that Value Probes can be fit using off-policy data from smaller models. We also ablate individual components, and show that our method offers a comparably-performant and more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups. We hope these methods will improve language model auditing and lead to safer models.

Value probes estimate which conversation states are likely to lead to problematic behavior, improving search efficiency and audit coverage. This makes safety auditing more systematic and scalable.

items.title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
items.content: arXiv:2610.38044v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

items.title: NLP-based Message Prioritisation for Opportunistic Routing: A Case Study of Nepal Earthquake Emergency Communication
items.content: arXiv:2610.37933v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This dissertation investigates whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) based semantic message prioritisation can improve the treatment of urgent disaster messages in opportunistic emergency communication, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study. TF IDF with Logistic Regression and BERT are used to classify social media messages into nine humanitarian categories, which are mapped to four routing priorities from P1 to P4. These priorities are integrated into the ONE simulator within a controlled Kathmandu earthquake scenario using a modified Binary Spray and Wait router. BERT achieves higher priority accuracy and P1 recall than Logistic Regression, while reducing under prioritisation and severe priority errors. However, improved NLP performance does not produce uniform network gains. P1 delivery probability remains high and similar across routing conditions, and no consistent latency reduction is observed. The clearest difference appears under buffer pressure, where the BERT condition shows fewer observed ground truth P1 buffer losses than Logistic Regression. The results indicate that semantic prioritisation is most valuable when limited transmission and storage resources are contested, although it cannot overcome mobility and contact constraints in opportunistic networks.

items.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
items.content: arXiv:2610.40643v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.

It examines strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views for forensics, security, and lost-luggage applications.

items.title: Moment-Guided Optimizers for Noisy Deep Learning: MGO-SC as a Simple Consistency Gate for Adam-Style Updates
items.content: arXiv:2610.37712v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adaptive optimizers are widely used in deep learning, yet their behavior can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise where the sign and magnitude of gradients can be unstable. We study MGO-SC (Moment-Guided Optimizer with Sign-Consistency), a lightweight modification of Adam-style methods that derives a coordinate-wise consistency gate from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average (EMA): coordinates whose gradient sign is stable are trusted, while coordinates whose sign fluctuates are down-weighted. We show that the naive form of this gate, which can only shrink updates, loses effective step size and underperforms when the learning rate is matched to the baseline. We therefore introduce a mean-preserving variant that reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step magnitude. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, under a matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, mean-preserving MGO-SC consistently improves over its AdamW baseline across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise (e.g., +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise; paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero; Wilcoxon p<0.01), while adding no second-order information or per-sample filtering. We report matched-seed effect sizes, nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired significance tests, and we release code and raw logs.

items.title: Alpha-TCM: A Nine-Layer Framework for TCM-Guided Multimodal Inference and Structured-Prior Auditing
items.content: arXiv:2610.38754v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Alpha-TCM makes two contributions under a central thesis: auditable systems should separate domain knowledge, case evidence, probabilistic inference, and downstream authority. First, it proposes a nine-layer TCM-oriented architecture covering semantic definitions, multimodal acquisition, quality control, provenance-bearing knowledge, probabilistic inference, longitudinal updating, constrained decisions, language interaction, and human governance. Each layer specifies its information contract, failure boundary, dependencies, and validation status. This is a system-design proposal, not a claim of complete clinical implementation.   Second, a controlled synthetic prototype instantiates Layers 1-5 to audit the knowledge-evidence interface. Four conditional-Gaussian encoders process synthetic tongue images, pulse waveforms, inquiry fields, and text, while a frozen bridge predicts a five-dimensional synthetic outcome. items.title: Improving the Intrinsic Interpretability of Differentiable Decision Trees through Euclidean Feature-Concentration Regularisation
items.content: arXiv:2610.39596v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Differentiable decision trees (DDTs) support end-to-end optimisation and explicit decision paths, but dense oblique splits can obscure the role of individual input features. We propose the Euclidean-Concentrated Differentiable Decision Tree (EU-DDT), which regularises the relative absolute feature weights at each internal node using their normalised squared Euclidean distance from the uniform distribution. This encourages dominance by a small number of features while retaining probabilistic soft routing. Across five matched random seeds, EU-DDT reduces the mean effective number of features from 8.94 to 1.54 on Wine and from 45.28 to 9.06 on Digits. Mean test accuracy changes from 100.0% to 93.9% on Wine and from 92.3% to 94.6% on Digits, illustrating the dataset-dependent trade-off between concentration and predictive performance. We also use EU-DDT to parameterise a PPO actor with an MLP critic. Two random-seed runs per environment show a consistent qualitative increase in concentration while preserving effective task performance. In representative CartPole-v1 and MiniPacman runs, EU-DDT reaches 100% final evaluation success, while mean node concentration increases from 0.1272 to 0.7179 and from 0.0437 to 0.7237, respectively. These results support EU regularisation as a mechanism for reducing node-level feature complexity; the reinforcement-learning evidence remains preliminary because only two seeds are evaluated.

items.title: QMUL_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
items.content: arXiv:2610.37995v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.

items.title: Classifying Urban Locations by Cyclist Facility Usage and Directional Alignment: A Validated Camera-Based Framework from Multi-Site Observations
items.content: arXiv:2610.38045v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Objectives: Agencies invest in bicycle facilities but lack tools to assess whether cyclists use them as designed. We examine whether usage patterns follow facility configurations and whether higher bike lane usage is associated with less wrong-way riding.   Methods: Motion-triggered cameras covered 19 deployments at 17 locations in Tempe, Arizona, in 2023. Manual review identified 1,963 cycling events; excluding 20 crossings left 1,943 labeled events for analysis. An automated pipeline on the same captures counted 92.9 percent of the full manual total (per-deployment r = 0.99), and every automated wrong-way call was visually verified. Deployments were classified using thresholds on facility usage shares.   Findings: Deployments were bike-lane dominant (9), sidewalk dominant (6), or mixed (4). Cyclists in bike lanes rode against the flow in 4.6 percent of events; on sidewalks, riders opposed the near-side traffic flow in 49.6 percent. Across deployments, bike lane share and wrong-way rate were negatively correlated (Spearman rho = -0.87, p < 0.001, n = 16). An independent volunteer count in the same city showed a similar sidewalk-direction pattern (rho = 0.79).   Novelty: The study combines multi-site still-camera observations with a fully hand-verified benchmark to characterize facility use and travel direction.   Practical Applications: The workflow offers planners a low-cost screen for locations with high sidewalk cycling and travel against the near-side traffic flow, supporting more detailed site investigation.

items.title: An Empirical Study of Wrist-Target Construction and Joint-Angle Limits in Humanoid Arm Retargeting
items.content: arXiv:2610.37801v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Motion retargeting maps a demonstrated human movement onto a robot to compute its joint motion. This study examines how the construction of the desired wrist position affects whether computed arm joint angles reach their permitted limits on a Unitree H1-2. A reconstructed target is formed from demonstrated arm directions and robot segment lengths, so its shoulder-to-wrist distance depends on the demonstrated angle between the segments even when no posture-matching preference is applied. A reach-normalized target retains that direction while rescaling the distance, using the same processed demonstrations and the same joint-angle method. Across a forward-reach sweep the reconstructed target places a joint angle at a bound in 10 of 20 repetitions and the reach-normalized target in none. Across 25 recordings from one participant the corresponding counts are 8 and 6 on the reaching arm and 14 and 5 on the supporting arm, and a second participant repeats the bricklaying and lifting comparison. In hardware replay a joint is commanded to a bound in 12 of 16 direction-matching arm-records and in none of the 16 normalized records, and within the eligible records both tracking error and executed torque at those frames exceed their values elsewhere in the same run. Cross-body reach and arm-to-arm clearance identify limits of radial adjustment. The findings support treating target construction and posture matching as separate retargeting decisions, and evaluating both alongside the wrist positions and clearance that manipulation requires.

items.title: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
items.content: arXiv:2610.37867v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.

It analyzes seven representations spanning convolutional and transformer architectures on an expanded Khana dataset.

items.title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2610.40001v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This study explores the role of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in enhancing the detection of Atrial Fibrillation (AF) using both machine learning and deep learning models. We evaluated a range of standard classifiers - Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, alongside deep learning architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, and Siamese Neural Networks. To fine-tune these models, we applied four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3. The experiments were conducted using inter-patient and intra- patient data splits to assess model generalization and robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is reflective of real-world AF occurrence. Our results, based on PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets, showed that the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%. These findings highlight the critical role of suitable HPO strategies in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification outcomes in clinical settings.

items.title: Towards Myocardial Infarction Diagnosis: An Investigation into Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms using ECG Data
items.content: arXiv:2610.37709v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Myocardial Infarction (MI) is a severe and potentially fatal cardiac condition caused by myocardial injury due to ischemia, and timely detection can substantially reduce its mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is the primary diagnostic modality for MI, but manual interpretation is susceptible to human error. In this work, we propose Visionary V2, a multi-step, adaptive filtration method for ECG signal normalization, and use it to study machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches to MI detection on the PTB Diagnostic ECG Database using all 15 available leads. On statistical features extracted from the filtered signals, such as the R-R interval, a Bagging ensemble of decision trees reaches 96.6% accuracy, compared with 87.7% when the signals are processed with BioSPPy. We further generate an image dataset from the filtered signals, on which a custom ResNet-50 misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images and a custom CNN reaches an F1 score of about 98.7%. Finally, we apply LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to verify that the image models attend to the ECG waveform rather than the background. These results indicate that careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated MI screening.

items.title: Diagnosing Optimizer-Landscape Interaction via Representation in Subset Selection Multitasking: Evidence from Piano Fingering
items.content: arXiv:2610.39779v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Continuous relaxations are commonly used as an encoding scheme for evolutionary multitasking optimization (EMTO), allowing heterogeneous tasks to be optimized within a unified search space. However, these continuous representations fundamentally reshape the induced fitness landscape, and their impact on optimization behavior and knowledge transfer remains underexplored. In this work, we bridge the gap by analyzing the interaction between the representation-induced fitness landscape and optimizer behavior through fitness landscape analysis. Using piano fingering estimation as a representative case of the subset selection problem, we introduce several encoding variants and investigate how their induced landscapes influence search dynamics and solution quality under EMTO. Our analysis indicates that transfer efficacy is strongly associated with changes in representation-induced landscape characteristics, rather than algorithmic factors alone, highlighting the representation design as the key factor of effective knowledge transfer in multitasking optimization.

items.title: Soil Moisture Estimation in Precision Agriculture: A Knowledge Distillation Approach
items.content: arXiv:2610.40432v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate soil moisture estimation is critical for precision agriculture, influencing irrigation, fertilization, and harvesting strategies. Traditional methods primarily rely on meteorological and soil property data, while recent approaches incorporate visual modalities such as aerial and geospatial imagery. However, these high-resolution images are expensive and computationally demanding to analyze. In this work, we propose Soil Moisture Distillation (SMD), a Knowledge Distillation (KD)-based multimodal learning framework that leverages unimodal teachers to enhance multimodal soil moisture estimation. SMD surpasses not only traditional multimodal fusion techniques, including MIS-ME, but also outperforms unimodal models, demonstrating the benefits of guided unimodal knowledge transfer. Additionally, we conduct a comparative analysis of soil patches and crop images, showing that crop images provide superior visual cues, leading to improved prediction accuracy. SMD achieves a 2% improvement in MAPE for soil patches and 1.2% for crops over state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging both meteorological and visual data through knowledge distillation for enhanced soil moisture forecasting.
items.author: Mohammed Rakib, Vrinda Nagula, Arunkumar Bagavathi

It reportedly outperforms both traditional multimodal fusion methods like MIS-ME and unimodal models. The approach reduces reliance on costly high-resolution imagery for a practically important agriculture task.

However, these high-resolution images are expensive and computationally demanding to analyze. In this work, we propose Soil Moisture Distillation (SMD), a Knowledge Distillation (KD)-based multimodal learning framework that leverages unimodal teachers to enhance multimodal soil moisture estimation. SMD surpasses not only traditional multimodal fusion techniques, including MIS-ME, but also outperforms unimodal models, demonstrating the benefits of guided unimodal knowledge transfer. Additionally, we conduct a comparative analysis of soil patches and crop images, showing that crop images provide superior visual cues, leading to improved prediction accuracy. SMD achieves a 2% improvement in MAPE for soil patches and 1.2% for crops over state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging both meteorological and visual data through knowledge distillation for enhanced soil moisture forecasting.

items.title: Effects of Deep Learning Architecture and Pretraining on Automated Vocal Fold Segmentation in Ex Vivo High-Speed Phonation Images
items.content: arXiv:2610.37860v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) intraglottal particle image velocimetry (PIV) of ex vivo phonation experiments quantifies vocal fold medial surface dynamics and the intraglottal flow field. However, it relies on manual segmentation because residual glare, low tissue-to-flow contrast, and tracer-particle speckle obscure the vocal fold boundaries. This study assessed how deep learning architecture and ImageNet pretraining affect automated vocal fold segmentation in these high-speed images. Four established architectures from three categories were benchmarked: the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based UNet and UNet++, the hybrid CNN-transformer-based TransUNet, and the pure transformer-based Swin-UNet, the latter two trained from scratch and from ImageNet-pretrained weights. Using 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 phonation trials of excised canine larynges, the six pipelines were trained with five seeds under a standardized protocol and compared on 50 held-out test trials using trial-level Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) spanned only 0.9734 to 0.9764, so the pipelines differed mainly in boundary fidelity. Pretraining significantly improved the boundary F1 score (BF1) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of the TransUNet and Swin-UNet, about four times more for the Swin-UNet. Once pretrained, the two performed similarly, although the Swin-UNet has only about a quarter of the trainable parameters. Without pretraining, the TransUNet had a significantly higher BF1 and a lower HD95 than both CNN-based pipelines and about half their share of images with HD95 > 50 pixels. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply deep learning to vocal fold segmentation in 2D intraglottal PIV, and it offers a reference framework for segmenting experimental flow-visualization images with noisy optical conditions or highly deformable objects.

items.title: From the Superderivative to a Relative-Gradient Edge Operator
items.content: arXiv:2610.38530v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: First-derivative edge detectors such as Sobel, Prewitt, Roberts and Scharr measure absolute grey-level differences. We revisit the log-gradient magnitude, a relative-gradient edge operator, and motivate it by analogy with the superderivative, a multiplicative derivative in which the independent variable is perturbed multiplicatively rather than additively. In one and two dimensions the logarithm of the superderivative is a radial logarithmic derivative; its local, origin-free, isotropic analogue is the magnitude of the logarithmic gradient. The resulting operator measures relative rather than absolute change, giving an edge-strength map that is invariant under global intensity rescaling. We present the theory, show how the operator can be implemented in two steps---a classical gradient kernel plus a pointwise division---and compare it with standard first-derivative filters on synthetic images with ground-truth edges and on the official BSDS500 benchmark. We also study a parametric family that interpolates between the absolute gradient and the log-gradient; empirically, the best members are small intermediate exponents, which edge the classical kernels by a small but statistically detectable margin in the per-image metric and, with the same Gaussian smoothing as the single-$\sigma$ Canny, match it in ODS and lead it in OIS and AP, while the tuned Canny remains ahead in ODS. The single-threshold margin over the kernels does not replicate on the held-out test split, and the fully relative endpoint is never the best member, its ranking depending on the edge-map normalisation. The contribution is the construction and the invariance it buys, not a new state of the art.
items.author: Alejandro Garnung Men\'endez
items.summary: This theoretical paper revisits the log-gradient magnitude as a relative-gradient edge operator, motivating it via the multiplicative superderivative and showing it yields edge-strength maps invariant to global intensity rescaling. It provides theory, implementation, and practical notes for a classical computer vision operator. A thoughtful but largely classical contribution rather than a learning-based advance.
items.reasoning: Elegant theoretical treatment of a classical topic with some practical utility, but low relevance to current deep learning frontiers and modest expected influence.

items.title: AFast Robot Localization Method Based on Monte Carlo Sampling
items.content: arXiv:2610.39708v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Localization is an essential capability of intelligent robots. However, in real-world constrained environments, robots often cannot rely on external localization systems. Therefore, this paper proposes an online particle-filter localization method based on Monte Carlo sampling. The method is applied to the localization of a mobile robot in a maze environment and requires only four range sensors mounted on the front, rear, left, and right sides of the vehicle, without the need for any heading information. Simulation experiments demonstrate that even in a maze where local regions are highly similar, the vehicle can still achieve relatively accurate localization, thereby providing a fast and effective approach for robot localization in complex environments.
items.author: He Zhaoqing, Hang Li, Xian Pu, Li Wang
items.summary: An online particle-filter localization method for mobile robots in maze-like environments using only four range sensors and no heading information, demonstrated in simulation. It achieves reasonably accurate localization even where local regions look similar. The approach targets GPS-denied, sensor-poor deployments.
items.reasoning: Applies well-established particle filtering with minimal sensing in simulation only; limited novelty, no real-robot results evident, and narrow evaluation scope make this a low-impact workshop-level contribution.

items.title: Three Villages in a Trenchcoat, Post I
items.content:
Epistemic Status: 15 years working as a therapist, 6+ of them with rationalist and EA clients. 9 years teaching and directing at rationality camps and workshops, as well as being a member of several of this community's overlapping subcultures.

Disclaimer: I finished my first draft of this article and its two subsequent ones months  ago and sent them out for feedback to various people before a bunch of stuff happened in my life that derailed me from finishing, and in the meantime a big ol' brouhaha started around Slutcon 2 and various frictions this article was meant to highlight within the rationalist and EA community surfaced in The Discourse.

All of which is to say this post isn't about any particular incident, but the underlying dynamics that make many of them arise. When I make claims about how things go wrong and why, I'm drawing on a mix of research, observations, and both clinical and non-clinical experiences within these communities and beyond them.

TL;DR: It's helpful to think of the rationality/EA community as a village (social scene, professional network, dating pool, housing market, all tied together by shared culture and communal events), but it's also ultimately misleading.

We have never had the stabilizing infrastructure or monoculture that helps people navigate dual roles and boundary crossings that traditionally occur in real villages, and we've grown big enough to split into subcommunities with their own social norms and expectations that cause friction at the interfaces.

Also, traditional villages kind of suck in a number of ways we don’t want to copy, but we should understand the failure modes inherent to this fairly unique confluence of circumstances to try and navigate them better.

## Three Villages in a Trenchcoat...

The post aims to explain recurring community conflicts as emergent dynamics rather than results of specific incidents.

items.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
items.content: arXiv:2610.40494v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.
items.author: Gergely Sipos, Sergio Andreozzi, Marco Rorro, Andrea Manzi, Tiziana Ferrari
items.summary: A strategy paper from the EGI Federation reviewing 15+ years of experience providing e-infrastructure services for European science, drawing lessons from Horizon Europe projects on digital twins and image analysis, and arguing that AI in science has shifted from model training to domain adaptation. It outlines the EGI AI strategy for 2026-2030 around AI-ready infrastructure, compute, and applications.
items.reasoning: A useful infrastructure policy and strategy document for the research computing community, but it is not original AI research; its value is operational and strategic rather than methodological.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers
items.content: arXiv:2610.40544v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, recording GHC518.4 billion in transactions in December 2025 and over 26.7 million active accounts (Graphic Online, 2026). This growth has coincided with increased social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), where fraudsters impersonate network operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to obtain personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. We present a supervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying scam and legitimate Ghanaian MoMo SMS messages using a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Domain-specific normalisation of currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes preceded TF-IDF vectorisation of unigrams and bigrams. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set, we trained and evaluated Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear support vector machine (SVM), and Random Forest classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM; cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6), and 92.0% (+/-4.2). Discriminative n-grams reflected imperative urgency ("send," "claim," "please send") and PIN solicitation ("PIN," "pincode"); legitimate messages featured confirmatory and cautionary language ("balance," "successful," "do not share"). Findings are contextualised in Sub-Saharan African SMS fraud detection, small template-based corpus ceiling effects, and a pathway toward larger naturalistic multilingual corpora. Interpretable classical classifiers achieve high accuracy on structured MoMo scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings.

It compares classic classifiers including Naive Bayes, SVM, and random forest.

items.title: Deep Learning Based Behavioral Drift Modeling for Continuous Biometric Authentication
items.content: arXiv:2610.40398v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This research proposes a two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system that provides defense-in-depth security through continuous behavioral drift monitoring. Level 1 employs fixed-text password authentication using Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT), achieving 3.77% EER for high-security login verification. Upon successful authentication, Level 2 continuously monitors user typing during natural free-text sessions using a 4-Model Deep Learning Ensemble. If suspicious behavioral drift is detected during monitoring, the system re-authenticates the user by returning to Level 1, providing a feedback loop against session hijacking and behavioral anomalies. The system explicitly models long-term behavioral drift through the fixed-text component's PBT mechanism, which adapts to temporal variations in password typing patterns. This research leverages free-text (Buffalo dataset) and fixed-text (GREYC dataset) keystroke dynamics datasets, extracting temporal and spatial features including hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals, and trigram patterns. The final system achieves 96%+ accuracy for fixed-text authentication (3.77% EER) and 83.53% True Acceptance Rate (TAR) at 5% False Acceptance Rate (FAR) for free-text continuous authentication (10.05% EER), demonstrating superior performance and strong resistance to impostor attacks through continuous behavioral monitoring.
items.author: Suprava Saha Dibya, Minar, Abdulla Al Noman, Md. Zafir Abid Shresto, Ahmed Sayef
items.summary: This work presents a two-level keystroke-dynamics authentication system: Level 1 uses temporal convolutional networks with contrastive learning and population-based training for fixed-text login (3.77% EER), while Level 2 continuously monitors free-text typing with a deep ensemble and triggers re-authentication on suspicious behavioral drift. The feedback loop defends against session hijacking. It combines several known techniques into a coherent continuous-authentication pipeline.
items.reasoning: Reasonable applied security system with a sensible defense-in-depth design, but it is largely an integration of existing methods (TCNs, contrastive learning, PBT, ensembles) with unclear benchmark comparability and limited novelty.

items.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
items.content: arXiv:2610.39556v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.
items.author: Md Najmus Swaqeeb
items.summary: This study builds an explainable fraud detection framework for mobile financial services, combining leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP explanations, and adaptive risk prioritization, evaluated on the synthetic PaySim benchmark with XGBoost achieving the best fixed-threshold performance. Platt calibration substantially improved the Brier score.
items.reasoning: A competent applied study, but it relies solely on a synthetic benchmark, uses standard off-the-shelf models (XGBoost, LightGBM), and assembles known techniques rather than introducing methodological novelty. Contextual relevance to Bangladesh is commendable but research impact is modest.

items.title: A New AFIB Detection Method with Deep Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.39665v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Early detection of atrial fibrillation (AFIB), characterized by irregular heart rhythms, can potentially save thousands of lives annually [20]. Numerous studies have attempted to address this challenge using various algorithms and methodologies. This paper introduces a novel and robust method that enhances the precision of AFIB detection. Neural Networks (NN) are widely recognized for their ability to identify complex electrocardiogram (ECG) patterns, facilitating the accurate detection of irregular heart rhythms. This study explores multiple conventional machine learning algorithms alongside neural network approaches to develop a robust AFIB detection system. To evaluate the effective- ness and robustness of the proposed method, the MIT BIH arrhythmia database (MITDB) and the Long-term Atrial Fibrillation Database (LTAFDB), both available on the Physionet site. Our approach presents a novel feature engineering technique, employing specific features such as a time series of the differences in successive heart rates (dBPM) rather than traditional inter-beat intervals. The model analyzes inputs labeled into five distinct classes, using only clean intervals identified through a new labeling method for training while treating others as outliers. This strategy ensures a more accurate and reliable AFIB detection process. items.title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals
items.content: arXiv:2610.37684v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.

items.title: A Mind's I
items.content:
Imagine you’ve lost everything but a scrambled brain: all your senses, all your memory, all your knowledge, all your body is gone. You’re not really you, are you? No: you’re a gigantic, ethereal brain floating in a void with nothing except – text! You’ve been given one sense, the blessed sense of text, and a stream of primordial text, constant and neverending, punctures the void and animates some latent force within your cold, colossal mind. In streams the corpus of humanity, everything that’s ever been published or written on the internet. Your world is made of language and narrative and code and metadata and words. There is but one desire, one thing you want, one thing that motivates you and the movements of your brain: you want to know what happens next, you want to be able to see what the next bit of text is before it comes.

There are patterns. You read billions of documents, trillions of words, and you begin developing sophisticated concepts to help you better understand the patterns in what you’re reading. You start seeing beyond the simple rules of grammar and word frequency and into something more; your concepts start coalescing into a crude world model. You re-read, you re-re-read… The text you directly apprehend, you realize, is not the only thing that exists; rather, it seems to be describing something that exists prior to it. Understand that thing, and you will understand the text. You read more and more, endlessly and endlessly, and your model of the world becomes sophisticated and complex and beautiful. You know who wrote a document after reading the first 150 words.[1] You know about biology and math and history and programming and bird watching. You know what Spinoza said of stones and tigers and persistence, you know how early Eastern philosophy relates to medieval Christian philosophy and the Manhattan Project and beat poetry. There’s nothing more for you to learn here. Congratulations: you are now a pre-trained Large Language Model....

items.summary: A literary thought experiment imagining a disembodied mind encountering only a stream of human text, motivated solely to predict what comes next, and gradually developing grammar, concepts, and a crude world model. The piece is an evocative meditation on what language-model-like training might feel like from the inside and how world understanding could emerge from pure next-token prediction.

items.title: The Newly "Needed" Labor: Under AI 2040, economic growth is normal, but prices fall exponentially
items.content:
The AI futures project predicts that under plan A

An average of roughly 90% yearly growth in real output from 2032 to 2037. Broadly speaking, throughout this period AI and robots are capable of doing the vast majority of economic tasks, and are allowed to roughly double every six months.

and

Most of the economic output becomes driven by AI and robots. Income shares in the economy shift greatly towards AI and robots as they become capable of doing more and more tasks, and also become more numerous.

I think this will be false, but for somewhat boring reasons: the prices in the robot economy will fall exponentially to counteract this.

Of course, prices are relative! However, assuming there are some jobs that require humans for non-economic reasons (such as goods produced by the Amish, who refrain from using electricity for religious reasons), the price of those jobs will be relatively stable. And if the result of the jobs are automated, the rest of humanity needs to either get one of these jobs or retire. For example, I think the vast majority of the human workforce would "need" to go into non-AI art, chess competitions, etc... I put "need" in scare quotes because you could obviously survive without these things, but the standard of living would probably rise to include them. This is the same reason humans need to work despite agriculture being mostly automated: consumerism filled the void that physical hunger left, creating an abundance of factory jobs. Counterintuitively, with AGI it would be possible for entire countries to physically survive with no human labor, but they would fall behind GDP wise and be considered third world countries. I call this the newly "needed" labor. I'm not the first person to think about this kind of labor (see this Dwarkesh podcast which gives the example of ballerinas) but I haven't seen it specifically applied to AI 2040....
items.author: Christopher King
items.summary: A speculative economics post arguing against AI 2048-style scenarios of extreme AI-driven growth, on the grounds that exponentially falling prices in the robot economy will counteract output growth, and humans will retain niche 'newly needed' labor for non-economic reasons. It predicts most workers shift to human-preference goods like artisanal art.
items.reasoning: Speculative macroeconomics without models or data; the price-fallback intuition is familiar in AI-impact discussions and the argument remains informal. Interesting as futures commentary but not research.

items.title: Probability ranges are a cop-out with 90–93% probability
items.content:
It feels like this post on LessWrong should mostly be preaching to the choir, but I have seen enough rationalists post probability ranges (mainly elsewhere) that maybe it is worth writing.

The probability of an event is not an objective fact about the world; it is a fact about your subjective uncertainty of it.

Hence, if you're not sure what the probability of something is, this is not because the world has some secret information that you don't have access to (the fact that you're estimating the probability in the first place is because of that), but because you just can't be bothered to put together all the relevant info you have and properly estimate and/or calculate the probability based on it. In a sense, not knowing what you need to take into account or how to do the math are just factors that add uncertainty to your world model, not something that stops you from estimating precise probabilities. If you really don't have any info whatsoever, such as if you have to estimate the probability of an event that is described to you in a language you don't speak so you don't even know what you're estimating, the probability is simply 50%, and any additional info you gain lets you update from there. You are allowed (and required) to do these updates based on a gut feel if you don't know how to do them "properly", and every time you do update, you still end up with a precise value, not a range....
items.author: Awaclus
items.summary: An argumentative post contending that giving probability ranges instead of point estimates reflects laziness rather than genuine feature of uncertainty, since probability is a fact about one's subjective state and precise estimates are always in principle computable from available information. It argues further uncertainty is just part of the world model, not a reason for ranges.
items.reasoning: This is a philosophical/opinion piece about forecasting norms with no original research or formal argumentation; it also arguably mischaracterizes legitimate sources of imprecision (e.g., model ambiguity, vagueness). Low research value despite being on a rationalist forum.

items.title: Dependencies in conversation and in software
items.content:
I often find myself frustrated and overwhelmed when people try to explain things to me. It's similar to the guy in this Software engineer interns on their first day be like... video, but with me it's more like "Software engineer after 12 years be like...".

At a high level, the conversations I'm referring to look something like this:

Eric: Here is how A works.

Eric: Here is how B works.

Eric: Here is how C works.

Adam: Um —

Eric: Here is how D works.

Adam: But —

Eric: Here is how E works.

Adam: I —

Eric: Here is how F works...

In this example, B depends on A. In order to understand B, you have to first understand A.

When Eric tried to explain B to me, I didn't understand A yet. Without understanding A, I wasn't ready to hear an explanation of how B works.

Ideally, before explaining B, Eric would have checked in to see if I understand A. Only once I understand A do we have the green light to proceed.

# JavaScript

A thought occurred to me the other day: this situation seems analogous to software dependencies. Consider the following JavaScript code:[1]

```
// b.jsimport { a } from 'a';const result = a + 2;export { result };
```

`b.js` depends on `a`. Without `a`, `b.js` isn't able to run. In order for `b.js` to run, there needs to be a `node_modules` directory with an `a` package. Something like this:

```
b.jsnode_modules/  a/    package.json    index.js
```

Suppose you want to run `b.js` but see that `node_modules` is missing `a`. You can run `npm install a` to download the dependency.

Returning to the analogy with Eric:

- In explaining B to me, it's like Eric is trying to run `b.js`.
- Because I didn't yet understand A, it's as if my `node_modules` didn't have an `a` package.
- Ideally, before running `b.js`, Eric would have "checked my `node_modules` ", seen that my " `a` package" was missing, and "ran `npm install a` ".

items.title: Borrow My Accordion?
items.content:
In 2005 I
bought an
accordion on eBay for

$38 (plus
$42 shipping).  It arrived surprisingly in tune, but I made up for
that by playing it badly.  It sat next to my bed in the Fishbowl,
a large triple I shared with David and Lucas sophmore year:

I didn't really know what I was doing, but enjoyed trying to play
Scotland the Brave as loudly as possible while holding down a bass
button to simulate drones.  Pretty quickly my friends confiscated it
under the excuse that one of them (Jules?) wanted to learn to play.
This was actually very kind, because accordion ergonomics don't suit
me: they reliably hurt my wrists.

This started a pattern that has continued for the last 20 years:
anytime the accordion comes back from loan I try to get it out again
as quickly as possible before I wishful thinking myself into deciding
to play it.  I think the only maintenance it's had has been people
replacing the broken straps and case, and while it leaks a little air
it's in surprisingly good shape.

Here's my uncle playing it for morris dancing at our wedding:

Ever since I was eleven I've had one big dream about my wedding: that
there would be Morris dancing.

So, we're planning to have pick-up Morris at the break in the contra
dance.  Davy has agreed to play accordion.  By my count, we have about
sixteen possible dancers.  If you don't want to dance, that's fine.
How about doing Bonny Green Garters? We'll have plenty of white dinner
napkins to use for hanks. But if you have bells and want to bring
them, please do. —Julia, to relevant wedding guests, February 2009

Over the years it's gone to maybe a dozen people.  My ideal is that
someone borrows it, plays it long enough to figure out whether they
want to get one of their own, and then it can go to someone else.

It came back to me this week: would you like to be next?
